part_title: Hybrid Evaluation, ROUGE, BLEU, BERTScore and Bedrock Jobs

scenes.title: Hybrid evaluation strategy
scenes.narration: This slide brings three evaluation methods together. Read the three columns from left to right. Human evaluation is strong at detecting nuanced problems: unsafe advice, bias, tone, user experience and domain-specific mistakes. Benchmark metrics test a stable dataset repeatedly, helping identify correctness problems and regressions after a model or prompt change. An LLM acting as a judge can assess relevance, clarity, reasoning and instruction following across a much larger collection of outputs. But each method has weaknesses. Humans are expensive and may disagree. Fixed benchmarks cover only what their datasets contain. A model judge can be biased or inconsistent. Now look at the release gate in the lower panel. The automated benchmarks and judge both show pass, but the human safety review finds an unsafe response. The correct decision is to block release until that issue is addressed. That's the teaching point: don't average away a serious safety failure just because the other scores look good. Choose evaluation methods based on risk and application requirements, and combine their evidence when deciding whether the release is ready.

scenes.title: ROUGE for Summarization
scenes.narration: Here we examine ROUGE, a metric commonly used to evaluate summaries. The left side explains that ROUGE compares word sequences, called n-grams, between the candidate summary and a human-written reference. In its recall-oriented form, it asks what fraction of reference n-grams the candidate covers. Now examine the worked example. The reference is 'The cat sat on the mat.' The generated text uses the same opening but ends with 'rug.' For ROUGE one, we count matching individual word tokens and divide by the six reference tokens, giving four out of six, approximately zero point six seven. For ROUGE two, we compare adjacent pairs. Four of the five reference bigrams match, giving zero point eight. Notice that different ROUGE variants measure different levels of lexical overlap. A high score suggests the wording covers much of the reference, but it doesn't prove the factual meaning is correct. A good paraphrase may receive a low ROUGE score simply because it uses different words. This is why we combine ROUGE with semantic checks and human review, especially for generative AI answers where the exact phrasing can vary.

scenes.title: BLEU for Translation
scenes.narration: This slide explains BLEU, another n-gram overlap metric, originally designed for machine translation. Compare the example across the top. The English source says the cat is sleeping on the mat. The shorter French candidate says 'Le chat dort sur le tapis,' while the reference expresses the same idea using a longer construction. BLEU focuses on the precision of candidate n-grams, using clipped matches so repeating a matching word cannot inflate the score without limit. Look at the table of one-gram through four-gram comparisons. The candidate may match all individual words and many pairs, but longer sequences begin to differ. The next panel adds the brevity penalty because an overly short translation could otherwise look artificially strong. In this example, the candidate has six words against eight in the reference. The worked calculation combines the n-gram precisions geometrically with a brevity penalty and yields an illustrative score around zero point six. The important limitation is that valid translations can use different words or sentence structures. BLEU is useful when comparing systems on consistent datasets, but it doesn't directly prove fluency, meaning or safety for an individual answer.

scenes.title: BERTScore for Semantic Similarity
scenes.narration: Now we move beyond matching exact words. The slide begins by turning each token into a contextual embedding, which represents a word in relation to the words around it. The similarity matrix in the middle compares tokens from a candidate sentence against tokens from the reference using cosine similarity. For each candidate token, BERTScore finds a strong match in the reference, helping compute precision. Reversing the direction gives recall, and their harmonic mean produces an F one score. Look at the examples on the right. 'A man is playing a guitar' and 'A person plays the guitar' use different words but receive a high semantic similarity score. A description of a child playing an instrument is also related, while a sentence about a cat sleeping on a sofa is much less similar. This shows what BERTScore can capture that BLEU or ROUGE may miss. However, similarity is not the same as factual correctness. Negation, numbers, specific names and small but critical changes can still fool a semantic metric. The embedding model and application domain also influence scores. Use BERTScore alongside task-specific factual tests and human evaluation.

scenes.title: Bedrock model evaluations
scenes.narration: This slide shows a practical evaluation workflow in Amazon Bedrock. Read the steps across the top. First choose the generator model whose responses you want to test. Then choose an evaluation method, such as an automated evaluator model or a human review workflow. Provide a prompt dataset stored in S3, choose the task and the metrics, configure the evaluation job and inspect its results. The middle panels show the decisions that affect the outcome: the dataset may contain prompts, optional reference answers and metadata; evaluation tasks include summarisation, question answering or text generation; and metrics can include relevance, factuality, helpfulness, safety and coherence. A job also requires appropriate IAM permissions and access to its data. The results panel compares model outputs and scores by task, not just a single universal number. Notice the sample results are illustrative, not a real benchmark establishing that one named model is always best. The practical workflow is to run representative tests, review low-scoring individual responses, compare alternatives and preserve the model version and evaluator configuration. A Bedrock evaluation provides evidence for a release decision, but it doesn't replace deployment monitoring or human assessment of high-risk failures.
